claims.claim: Transportation was the largest source of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions in 2022, accounting for 28% of the total (29% when electricity used by the sector is included).

Within U.S. transportation in 2022, light-duty vehicles (passenger cars plus light-duty trucks) produced 57% of sector GHG emissions, medium- and heavy-duty trucks 23%, aircraft 9%, ships and boats 3%, and rail 2%; most of these emissions are CO2 from burning petroleum-based gasoline and diesel.

In 2019, personal vehicles averaged 0.47 pounds of CO2 per passenger-mile, and on average rail transit, passenger railroads, commercial air travel, and buses each emitted less per passenger-mile than personal vehicles; but intensity varies widely within a mode, e.g. transit buses averaged 0.95 lb/passenger-mile when lightly occupied while intercity motorcoaches averaged 0.15.

Argonne National Laboratory's R&D GREET 2024 model estimates that a 2025 electric vehicle produces about 46% fewer life-cycle GHG emissions than a comparable gasoline (internal-combustion) vehicle, using E10 gasoline for the gasoline car and the U.S. average grid mix for the EV; the assessment counts vehicle and battery production, fuel production, and use.

Manufacturing an EV, especially its battery, can create more emissions than manufacturing a gasoline car, but over the vehicle's lifetime total emissions from making, charging, and driving an EV are typically lower because EVs have zero tailpipe emissions; how much lower depends on the local electricity grid mix.

Because an EV's operating emissions track the grid that charges it, the same electric sedan in 2020 was estimated at 0.15 lb CO2/mile in California versus 0.33 lb CO2/mile in Colorado; as the grid decarbonizes, GREET projects the 2050 EV at 77 gCO2e/mile against 306 gCO2e/mile for the 2050 gasoline vehicle, widening the gap.

The Avoid-Shift-Improve (A-S-I) framework organizes transport policy into avoiding or reducing motorized trips, shifting remaining travel to more efficient modes (public transit, walking, cycling), and improving the technology and fuels of the vehicles that remain.

U.S. light-duty vehicles are governed by two parallel federal programs: Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, set in miles per gallon by NHTSA (Department of Transportation) under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act of 1975, and greenhouse-gas tailpipe standards, set in grams of CO2 per mile by EPA under the Clean Air Act (first adopted for 2010); the MY2026 CAFE rule targets a fleet-wide average near 49 mpg.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether public transit is automatically lower-emitting than driving.
positions: On average across the U.S., rail, air, and bus travel each emitted less CO2 per passenger-mile than personal vehicles in 2019 (CBO).
Intensity depends on occupancy: a lightly loaded transit bus averaged 0.95 lb/passenger-mile in 2019, more than the 0.47 lb personal-vehicle average, while a full motorcoach was 0.15 (CBO).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are true. The lesson states the average finding and immediately qualifies it: the mode's per-passenger-mile advantage is realized only when vehicles carry enough people. It avoids the greenwashing claim that transit is unconditionally cleaner.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether EVs are 'clean' given battery manufacturing and grid electricity.
positions: EVs shift emissions upstream: making the battery raises manufacturing emissions, and charging emissions depend on the grid (EPA; CBO).
Even so, life-cycle emissions are typically lower than a gasoline car's (~46% lower for a 2025 EV on the U.S. average grid per GREET), and fall further as the grid decarbonizes (EPA; Argonne GREET).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the honest trade-off — higher build emissions, grid-dependent charging — and the net result that lifetime emissions are generally lower, attributing each figure to GREET, EPA, or CBO and dating it.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft treated 'Sustainable Transportation' as a generic organizing concept with no data, no modal comparison, no EV analysis, and no policy naming. All of that boilerplate was discarded and replaced with dated, sourced content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced placeholder definitions with the EPA 2022 sector share (28%) and modal breakdown.
Added an honest, occupancy-aware treatment of per-passenger-mile intensity using CBO 2019 data, including the case where a transit bus exceeds a car.
Represented the EV question with both the lifecycle-lower finding (GREET/EPA) and the manufacturing and grid-mix caveats, with figures dated.
Named the actual U.S. standards (CAFE by NHTSA, GHG standards by EPA) and the Avoid-Shift-Improve framework at a naming level rather than asserting policy positions.
rightsIssues: Sources are U.S. federal agency works (EPA, DOE/Argonne, NHTSA/AFDC, CBO — public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105), one reputable NGO analysis (C2ES, reference-only), and one intergovernmental/development-community explainer of A-S-I (TUMI/SUTP/GIZ, reference-only). All lesson prose is original synthesis; no source wording reproduced beyond short attributed factual figures.
